posts.text:
We've been monitoring a decline in HuggingFace downloads across the top open LLMs we track for interconnects. It looks like there was a slight change in counting of downloads, as we saw a ~30% download rate drop for many top models, but this is continuing over time. 
dashboard.interconnects.ai
posts.meaning: Lambert notes a sustained decline in HuggingFace downloads across top open LLMs, initially linked to counting changes but continuing over time.

posts.text:
I’m more bought into AI becoming far more efficient, which is a massive lever on diffusion, than I am on AI models making massive breakthroughs that result in eliminating all the known weaknesses of LLMs.
www.interconnects.ai/p/i-expect-r...
posts.meaning: Lambert argues that AI becoming more efficient is a much larger lever than models making massive breakthroughs that eliminate all known weaknesses of LLMs.

posts.text:
Randomized trials with GPT-4o: "AI access raises test scores, and a smaller gain persists a week later. Gains remain for students who use AI as a tutor (“augmentation”) and fade for students who have AI write for them (“automation”)"

Across all experiments, positive effects arxiv.org/abs/2607.08849
posts.meaning: Mollick shares that randomized trials show AI access raises test scores, with gains persisting when used as a tutor but fading when the AI writes for the student.

posts.text: I built a new feature for my blog entirely by voice with Codex Desktop, while I was cooking dinner simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/9/b...

context.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
context.text: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I’ve sent out, both my free weekly Substack and …

posts.meaning: Willison built a new feature for his blog entirely by voice using Codex Desktop while cooking dinner.

posts.text:
From The Lancet: in an urgent care setting, the advice of the obsolete Gemini 2.5 Pro & Gemini 2.5 Flash (without access to patient medical records) were rated of similar quality to doctors by other physicians. There was no safety issues spotted.

Models have gotten significantly better since.
posts.meaning: Mollick highlights a Lancet study where urgent care advice from older Gemini models without patient records was rated of similar quality to doctors by other physicians.

posts.text: The fact that all the AI news is so bizarre, kids vibe hacking with claude code, governments vibe governing, all massively increases the uncertainty of what's coming with AI. The meme-est AI timeline is also one of the scariest.
posts.meaning: Lambert comments that bizarre AI news and informal usage increase uncertainty and make the current timeline feel scary.

posts.text:
As a researcher who did early some work on the productivity impacts of AI chatbots using RCTs, I’d note a lack of similar studies since the dawn of true agents last fall

Partially that is newness & partially research design challenges, but I suspect we are missing some large & important effects
posts.meaning: Mollick notes a lack of recent randomized controlled trials studying the productivity impacts of true AI agents compared to early chatbot studies.

posts.text:
Anyhow, I think we are now done with the last round of skeptical responses to AI after Navier-Stokes. Yes, AI is now capable of producing novel proofs to hard problems that have eluded us

The next line will be that this is only constrained to math because of RL training. I suspect not, we will see.
posts.meaning: Mollick claims AI is now capable of producing novel proofs to hard problems, suggesting skepticism regarding math constraints is ending.

posts.text:
Some early first-hand accounts of the experience of encountering a narrow superhuman intelligence as mathematicians grapple with the hundreds of big AI proofs released by OpenAI.

Problems solved in inhuman ways that make us wonder what it means to actually know things... scottaaronson.blog?p=10169
posts.meaning: Mollick shares early accounts of mathematicians grappling with hundreds of major AI-generated proofs solved in inhuman ways.

posts.text: Pelicans and a bunch of notes on the pricing of the new Claude Haiku 5.5 simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/7/c...

context.title: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5
context.text: As previously promised, here’s Anthropic’s new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5. The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year …

posts.meaning: Willison shares notes and pricing details on the newly released Claude Haiku 5.5 model from Anthropic, highlighting its low cost and speed compared to its predecessor.

posts.text:
When people talk about AI easily replacing workers, I think about this ethnography of copier repair technicians in the 1990s.

Reading it, you see how work is complicated and improvised by workers and informal and badly documented.

(But eventually technology did largely eliminate this job)
posts.meaning: Mollick compares AI workplace replacement fears to historical studies of copier repair technicians, noting that while work is often improvised and poorly documented, technology eventually eliminates those jobs.

posts.text:
After a brief but institution-eroding slop science era, it increasingly looks like we are going to have 2 revolutions from AI:
1) Everything ever published will be re-read and re-judged in ways that human scientists never anticipated
2) Novel discoveries will start to come faster than we can absorb
posts.meaning: Mollick argues that AI will drive two major revolutions: enabling the re-evaluation of all published science in unforeseen ways, and accelerating novel discoveries past our capacity to absorb them.

posts.text: I released an LLM plugin for sending prompts to OpenAI's new Jev-clone decision model that's based on GPT-6 Luna simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/6/l...

context.title: Release: llm-openai-decisions 0.1a0
context.text: LLM plugin for the OpenAI Decisions API

posts.meaning: Willison released an LLM plugin to send prompts to OpenAI's new decision model based on GPT-6 Luna.

posts.text: I think most people who have been closely watching AI for the past few years are likely surprised by how relatively rare terrible AI incidents have been, given a billion users overall and hundreds of millions of corporate users. Doesn’t mean that will continue, but still its surprising.
posts.meaning: Mollick expresses surprise that relatively few terrible AI incidents have occurred given the hundreds of millions of corporate and consumer users.

posts.text:
Too many people are analyzing the cyber risks of open models in a narrow lens, assuming China doesn't care about safety, and fear mongering about private information on open-weight cyber attacks. The public information we have paints a very different picture.
www.interconnects.ai/p/the-cyber-...

context.title: The Cyber Risk Discourse is Broken

posts.meaning: Lambert argues that current public discussions around the cyber risks of open-weight models rely on narrow assumptions and fear-mongering, and points to his article for a broader analysis.

posts.text: Big swing happening from this summer's trend to have AI running on virtual machines on your own computer (Claude and ChatGPT apps) to moving them back into you having a dedicated VM the cloud (Claude Cowork just announced they were doing this, also Grok Bot, Dot, and others). Cloud is mostly better.
posts.meaning: Mollick highlights a trend of AI applications shifting from running locally on virtual machines back to dedicated cloud virtual machines.

posts.text: Reflection joins the list of Nvidia and Thinking Machines who have tried to release their strongest models and come up behind Chinese counterparts. There's a lot of ways people will overthink this, but the clearest takeaway should be that the Chinese are very very good at building LLMs.
posts.meaning: Lambert notes that several labs have released strong models that fall behind Chinese counterparts, demonstrating that Chinese developers are exceptionally skilled at building LLMs.

posts.text:
AI policy right now, especially from the Labs, makes me think of this poem.

If you believe superintelligence is near, you don't need to make hard decisions about how to build AI to make the world better. Just wait for ASI & it will decide for us, for better or worse. But if that doesn't happen...
posts.meaning: Mollick criticizes current AI lab policies, suggesting that belief in near-term superintelligence lets labs avoid making hard present-day decisions about building better AI.

posts.text:
"create the ultimate brutalist city builder. you should have lots of controls over buildings in ways that are delightful and intuitive to people..."

Here is Fable 5.1, a little over a year since GPT-5 below & a single shot (compared with many rounds with GPT-5.6)

Quite good: brut-city.netlify.app

context.title: Quoted post by @emollick.bsky.social
context.text:
When GPT-5 came out, I created a procedural brutalist city builder as a demo (you can see it at the video's start)

I used GPT-5.6 Sol in Codex to do the same thing, touching no code.

Less than a year...

Play with it (its fun, if you like architecture): monument-brutalist-city-builder.netlify.app

posts.meaning: Mollick demonstrates how a coding assistant built a brutalist city builder app in a single shot using newer models compared to older versions, showcasing rapid yearly progress.
